title: The forest of ogresses
hookLine: a prince crosses a forest of temptations without looking back (Jataka 96)

cards: The road to the throne runs straight through a forest, and the forest is not empty. Along the way, the tale says, ogresses wait, and they don't look like monsters.

They build pleasant houses by the road, spread soft couches, and call sweetly to anyone passing. A young prince sets out to cross it anyway, because holy men have told him one thing: keep walking, and don't look at them.

teach.b: First, the warning. The prince is told the ogresses will tempt travelers through every door of the senses: sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touch. Whoever stops to look is lost.

Second, the companions. A few men insist on coming, sure they can manage. One by one they fall behind: one for a lovely form, one for a song, one for a sweet scent, one for a fine meal, one for a soft bed.
The ogresses take each of them. Third, the one who follows. The prince walks on alone.

teach.h: ONE FOLLOWS HIM TO THE CITY.
teach.b: One ogress follows him all the way to the city, telling everyone she's his wife. He never so much as glances at her. She ends up in the king's palace, and the story turns dark for the king who took her in.

The prince, who never turned his head, ends up on the throne. Fourth, the bowl of oil. The tale is called the Telapatta Jataka, the bowl-of-oil birth story, and it's linked to a teaching in the Samyutta Nikaya.

teach.h: A BOWL OF OIL, FULL TO THE BRIM.
teach.b: There, a man must carry a bowl filled to the brim with oil through a crowd watching a well-known beauty dance, while a man with a drawn sword walks behind him, ready to strike if a drop spills.
The Buddha says the bowl stands for mindfulness of the body. Both stories make the same point. The trouble isn't that the lure is there; it's turning toward it.
Attention is where the danger lies, and where the protection lies too.

how: In Buddhist practice this is called guarding the sense doors: noticing a sight or a sound without being pulled after it, trained in both walking and sitting meditation.

o: a holy woman who guides lost travelers
a female yakkha, an ogress of the wild
a queen who rules a forest kingdom

games.q: the forest of ogresses: tap the pairs.
p: stop to look, and are lost

s: they appear lovely and inviting: pleasant houses, soft couches, sweet voices.
one ogress follows the prince all the way to the city
she tells people she's his wife. he never looks at her.
in the bowl-of-oil teaching, a swordsman walks behind the man carrying it
he's ready to strike if a single drop spills.

games.q: you're a companion walking with the prince. by the road: a lovely house, a soft couch, a sweet voice calling you in. what do you do?
o: keep your eyes on the road and walk on.
go in to warn the others.
games.why: the companions who stopped were taken one by one. only the prince, who never looked, reached the city.

practice: Sit, and let something tempt you, a phone face down nearby, a snack in the kitchen, a plan for tomorrow, and when it calls, notice the picture, the sound, the pull.
Don't turn your head; come back to the breath, steady and full, like the man carrying the oil. You can know the lure is there and still walk past it.

wordCard.voice: Yakkhini. A female yakkha, an ogress of the wild places: what filled the forest a prince crossed by keeping his eyes on the road, while those who stopped to look were lost. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: yakkhini, a female yakkha, a spirit or ogress of the wild places.

carryVoice: Your line: don't look back. The prince kept his eyes on the road. See you tomorrow.
